findings.title: Blocked email matching is case-sensitive, allowing bypass
findings.body: Emails are case-insensitive. The lookup `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` does an exact, case-sensitive comparison. An attacker can bypass a block by using a different case (e.g., if 'bad@spam.com' is blocked, submitting 'Bad@Spam.com' will not match). The uniqueness validation on line 5 is also case-sensitive, allowing duplicate entries with different cases. Normalize emails to lowercase both when storing and when querying.

findings.title: should_block? increments match_count non-atomically and writes on every validation
findings.body: The method loads the record, increments `match_count` in memory, and saves the whole record. Concurrent requests for the same email can race, causing lost increments (both read the same value and write the same incremented value). Additionally, every call to `should_block?` for a matching email performs a database write, which an attacker can trigger repeatedly to amplify write load and potentially cause contention. Use an atomic `update_counters` or `update_all` to increment the counter and avoid saving the whole record.

findings.title: Missing tests for email domain whitelist/blacklist logic
findings.body: The domain restriction logic (whitelist/blacklist) was moved from User#email_validator to EmailValidator, but the new spec only tests the blocked email branch. There are no tests covering the whitelist/blacklist behavior, so regressions in that existing functionality could go unnoticed.
